method: Normal Look action; room-specific semantic hotspot, matching displayed description and served SHA-256.

observations.label: Directional antenna and alignment cradle
observations.observed: The antenna points into a stone buttress at arrival. Its original unaligned path is explicitly unsuitable. The cradle lets you align the existing surveyed path or restore the original position. The supplied survey declares the aligned outcome viable; no propagation calculation is being inferred. Matching endpoint settings is a separate check.

observations.label: Radio mast and maintenance ladder
observations.observed: The mast stands behind a safe waist-high railing. Its tagged cables lead to both endpoint cards. You can inspect and adjust the supplied alignment cradle from the walkway; no climbing, timing challenge, ally or side-quest reward is required to reach the controls.

observations.label: Alignment scope and survey card
observations.observed: A paper survey beside the scope distinguishes the unsuitable original position, a viable aligned existing path and a viable alternate path. Read and keep the survey, then inspect the selected result with the reusable kit. A path label records a proposal; the actual preparation check is still yours to perform.

observations.label: Path-clearance model and alternate path
observations.observed: A hinged model opens a second surveyed corridor beside the buttress. Selecting this alternate path is equally valid: its viable outcome is supplied by the exercise, not guessed from a drawing or signal strength. The same endpoint-settings requirement remains. You may switch back without losing a tool.

observations.label: Short-range beacon
observations.observed: The Blue Dragon has polished this small beacon until it resembles a jam jar with ambitions. Its card describes a separate short-range exhibit. A visible beacon does not prove that the directional path reaches the intended endpoint, and this optional exhibit holds no required reward.

observations.label: Radio selector and endpoint settings cards
observations.observed: Two cards list the exercise endpoints: fictional band WELL, scenario channel A initially, and PHY RELAY at both ends in the matched setting. The original test setting puts the far endpoint on fictional band OTHER, explicitly incompatible. Match the band, channel and PHY together. Later channel A/B choices move both channel selectors while preserving the selected matched or mismatched band/PHY state.

observations.label: Polarization exhibit
observations.observed: Two ribbons beside a model antenna invite comparison of orientation. This is an unscored conceptual exhibit; no numerical polarization penalty has been supplied. Follow the reviewed path and settings cards for the exercise rather than inventing a hidden threshold from the ribbons.

observations.label: Signal banner
observations.observed: The banner reads: STRONG IS NOT THE SAME AS CLEAR. Path viability and compatible settings prepare this fictional link; they provide no SNR, throughput or service guarantee. The Storm Observatory compares received signal with noise at the same boundary and requires a fresh test.

observations.label: Relay cabinet and tool-return card
observations.observed: The cabinet holds the alignment handles and a copy of the tool-return card. Your ordinary inspection kit is never consumed; if absent, return through the Workshop to the Arrival Lift and obtain it there. Both paths use supplied equipment. Notebook method, worked-step and solution hints remain available without penalty.

observations.label: Wireless bridge preparation terminal
observations.observed: The terminal asks you to check the selected path and endpoint settings separately. Record a real preparation reading and submit it; reading a survey or moving the antenna alone does not complete the investigation. A successful preparation still leaves signal/noise validation for the Observatory.

observations.label: Storm radar dish
observations.observed: The dish pivots above a weather chart whose arrows are explicitly illustrative. This room supplies a bounded interference exercise, not a radar, weather or electromagnetic propagation simulation. The current path and endpoint settings must still pass before an SNR result can validate the relay.

observations.label: Local interference emitter and isolation switch
observations.observed: The initially connected local emitter supplies raised-noise conditions on both fictional channel labels: signal −65 dBm, noise −78 dBm, SNR 13 dB. Isolate the emitter to restore the surveyed conditions, or reconnect it to repeat the failure. This is an authored change to the exercise; changing channel alone does not isolate it. After changing it, measure again.

observations.label: Observation telescope
observations.observed: The telescope points back toward the Skywell mast and the alternate surveyed corridor. A clear-looking image cannot supply a missing path check. Return to the Skywell if the antenna is unaligned or endpoint settings mismatch; a high numerical SNR never overrides either fault.

observations.label: Noise-floor meter and boundary exercise card
observations.observed: The meter reports comparable received power levels in dBm; their difference is an SNR in dB. The separately labeled supplied boundary exercise uses −65 dBm signal and −84.99 dBm noise: 19.99 dB fails the fictional inclusive 20 dB minimum, even if a display rounds it. This exercise replaces the supplied observation conditions; it is not a measurement of a production path. Return to surveyed conditions with the emitter isolation control, then measure again.

observations.label: Propagation globe
observations.observed: Colored paths wrap around the globe, with a clear legend: conceptual illustration only. No distance, terrain, rain attenuation or universal coverage calculation is scored here. The exercise supplies path outcomes and comparable power observations explicitly; real equipment needs its own specifications.

observations.label: Weather vane and diary shelf
observations.observed: The vane rattles above the Weather Diary. Open the optional diary to compare actual radio observations in recorded order. Old readings remain historical; a current comparison needs a new measurement after a change. The essential path, settings and noise evidence stays readable without hearing the vane.

observations.label: Satellite orbital model
observations.observed: A brass satellite circles a painted planet in the illustration. Its label offers a distance perspective without claiming that this room simulates a satellite network. The Celestial Eagle has underlined the words OPTIONAL EXHIBIT. Your current relay can be checked without solving another technology.

observations.label: Microwave reflector
observations.observed: The reflector bears a maintenance tag that points back to the supplied path survey. Its shape alone does not establish compatibility, received power or throughput. No unreviewed gain value, propagation penalty or alignment tolerance is hidden in this display.

observations.label: Signal history drum
observations.observed: The drum has separate BEFORE and AFTER columns. Actual readings remain in the notebook with their original conditions; old measurements stay stale after channel, path, settings or emitter changes. Returning to the same controls does not refresh an old reading. A mitigation proposal is not a measurement, and a path check is not endpoint service recovery.

observations.label: Channel survey desk and relay test
observations.observed: Under surveyed conditions, scenario channel A supplies −65 dBm signal and −90 dBm noise: 25 dB SNR. Scenario channel B supplies −65 dBm and −85 dBm: exactly 20 dB, an equally valid inclusive boundary. These fictional labels are not real channel recommendations or permanent rankings. Choose either at both endpoints, inspect the current path/settings and measure again. Passing this supplied SNR threshold does not prove throughput or service recovery.

observations.label: Twisted-pair cutaway
observations.observed: A transparent cutaway lets you follow the paired strands to their labeled contacts. The nearby card names the required terminations. Copperhead has drawn a tiny pair of spectacles over the words CHECK BOTH ENDS. Appearance helps you follow the path; the supplied compatibility and conductor tests decide whether this exercise passes.

observations.label: Copper patch panel and bench cards
observations.observed: The sender, receiver, copper medium and terminations are declared compatible for this fictional exercise. A matching plug shape is only one clue; read the supplied compatibility card. Both repair paths use this same matched equipment. The patch panel separates the original test section from the replacement stock so you can investigate without risking a working network.

observations.label: Cracked original section
observations.observed: The original path is 95 m + 10 m: 105 m in all, 5 m beyond the fictional inclusive 100 m maximum. The supplied diagnosis identifies a break in a required conductor of this cracked section. Record an actual inspection before changing it. A crack you can see is useful evidence here because the bench diagnosis names this section; an open reading alone would not locate every real fault.

observations.label: Short replacement path
observations.observed: A tray elbow leads to clean replacement stock. The bench handle replaces the diagnosed section and selects 85 m + 10 m: 95 m total, leaving 5 m below the fictional limit. The inspection kit checks the result; it does not mend copper. Choose this path, inspect compatibility, length and every required conductor, then submit the reading for preparation.

observations.label: Pair separator and damaged plug
observations.observed: The separator holds the tagged pairs beside a damaged plug, leaving each contact visible. The plug is an inspection clue, not an automatic verdict. The known fault in this exercise is the diagnosed open conductor in the cracked section; replacing unrelated parts cannot make that break disappear.

observations.label: Interference motor and shielding sample
observations.observed: The motor rattles under a shielding cross-section. Its maintenance card asks you to consider the physical surroundings; it supplies no interference measurement or shielding score. Noise you can hear is not a measurement of electrical interference. The diagnosed open conductor remains a separate, testable fault even while the motor makes its theatrical complaint.

observations.label: Tool and return card
observations.observed: Your reusable inspection kit is never consumed. If it is not in your satchel, the Arrival Lift remains reachable through the workshop and its kit is available without a side quest. The bench supplies both repair paths. The notebook offers method, worked-step and solution hints; using them does not make a technically valid repair less valid.

observations.label: Continuity pedestal
observations.observed: A handwritten instruction reads: TEST FIRST; KEEP THE BAD NEWS. The ordinary inspection kit reports total channel length and open required conductors for the selected path. Keep the actual open-before reading for the Echo Cavern. After either repair, inspect again; a remembered pass from another path does not test this one. The original section can be restored to the test bench if you need to recover a missed before reading.

observations.label: Alternate path and route-length wheel
observations.observed: The other tray takes a broad turn around the cracked section: 90 m + 10 m, exactly 100 m. The fictional limit includes equality, so this intact compatible path is just as valid as the 95 m choice. Zero length headroom is not an extra failure rule. Turn the bench selector, inspect the whole supplied passive path and use that reading when you submit.

observations.label: Fiber grove trunk
observations.observed: A glassy trunk divides into fine, labeled fibers. The illuminated branches represent light transmission, not electricity delivered to the far end. A maintenance ribbon points back to the workshop and its always obtainable inspection kit. No ally or optional reward is needed to follow this route.

observations.label: Light blossom cluster
observations.observed: The blossoms brighten when the exhibit is powered. Photon has hung a card among them: PRETTY IS NOT A MEASUREMENT. Visible light and a power indicator cannot establish a compatible data link, receiver reserve or working service. The useful evidence is written at the dock.

observations.label: Connector inspection dock
observations.observed: Inspect the original connection before changing it. The dock supplies a diagnosed connection defect for which both cleaning and compatible connector replacement are suitable. This is a declared exercise, not a field maintenance recipe. The reusable inspection tool observes; the dock and its stock perform the intervention. Reinspect afterward to confirm removal. Returning the original diagnostic connection lets you inspect and try again without erasing notes.

observations.label: Cleaning station
observations.observed: A tiny brush stands beneath an enormous sign reading PATIENCE IS A TOOL. In this supplied scenario the cleaning station can remove the diagnosed defect after inspection. The adjacent replacement tray is an equally valid intervention. Neither choice is a reward for recruiting a creature. After the dock acts, reinspect to confirm removal; a choice alone is not a passing preparation reading.

observations.label: Optical patch shelf and profile cards
observations.observed: The supplied candidate cards explicitly compare five fields: fiber/media, wavelength direction, supported rate, connector/polarity and host support. The initial candidate has a wavelength-direction mismatch. One card matches all five; each other candidate fails exactly its named field. Choose a proposed set before intervention, without inferring compatibility from shell shape or a light level. After intervention, restore the original diagnostic connection to choose another set and inspect again.

observations.label: Fiber bend exhibit
observations.observed: A wide loop and a pinched loop hang beside an intentionally unnumbered caution card. Real fiber handling and bend limits depend on the specified product. This exhibit supplies no universal bend radius or extra loss to add: the Prism Vault declares each path’s complete total loss. Do not quietly count this illustration as another measured component.

observations.label: Split fiber coupler
observations.observed: The coupler resembles a fork used by a very precise giant. Its branches illustrate a physical arrangement, not extra guaranteed payload channels. The supplied path totals already include every modeled loss. The exhibit offers no unsupported splitter gain, amplification or promise of free capacity.

observations.label: Broken fiber stump
observations.observed: The stump displays a separate visible break, labeled EXHIBIT ONLY. Cleaning cannot repair a physically broken strand. The active dock instead names a diagnosed connection defect with two suitable interventions. Match the intervention to that stated diagnosis; do not copy a remedy merely because two things look damaged.

observations.label: Optical receiver altar
observations.observed: The receiver altar has room for a lantern and a much more useful notebook. Complete inspection, intervention and reinspection at the dock, then use a fresh preparation reading. Receiver range and reserve still need their own Prism Vault proof; a compatible connection does not complete the optical budget.

observations.label: Photon lantern and maintenance ribbon
observations.observed: The lantern lights a fragment of the old maintenance ribbon. Its faded marks hint at a later optional record investigation, but no missing record blocks the garden. Method, worked-step and solution hints remain available from the objective panel, and assistance never makes a technically valid repair less valid.

observations.label: Prism engine
observations.observed: The engine turns slowly behind a window, projecting a line instead of an answer. Its transmitter is fixed at −3 dBm in this fictional exercise. Passive loss subtracts from that level; it cannot create optical gain. Prepared matching equipment and a fresh power measurement are separate requirements.

observations.label: Wavelength combiner
observations.observed: The combiner gathers colored lines into one display. The Rainbow Serpent’s exhibit illustrates wavelength multiplexing, not a guarantee that any colored module interoperates. Your supplied pair must match its required wavelength directions along with media, rate, connector/polarity and host support.

observations.label: Spectrum window
observations.observed: Colored stripes are mirrored by printed wavelength-direction labels so color is never the only evidence. Those labels refer to the supplied candidate profiles; no real wavelengths or product ranges are invented here. A favorable numerical budget cannot rescue a mismatched direction.

observations.label: Attenuation dial and passive-path selector
observations.observed: The fictional transmitter is −3 dBm. Path A totals 8 dB loss, giving −11 dBm receive and 3 dB reserve above −14 dBm sensitivity. Path B totals 9 dB loss, giving −12 dBm receive and exactly 2 dB reserve. Both meet the inclusive 2 dB requirement and the independent −1 dBm maximum. The initial high-loss path totals 10 dB: −13 dBm receive has only 1 dB reserve and fails. Select a path, then measure again; the dial does not make a reading.

observations.label: Splice enclosure
observations.observed: The enclosure’s clear lid reveals a neatly labeled join. It offers no new repair procedure or secret bonus. Every modeled component is already included in the declared total path loss. The active connection inspection and its suitable interventions remain at the Photon Gardens dock.

observations.label: Optical attenuator and overload comparison
observations.observed: A separate comparison card supplies an independent observed receive level of 0 dBm. It exceeds the fictional receiver’s −1 dBm maximum by 1 dB: more received power is not always safer. This is not produced by the passive −3 dBm transmitter exercise and is not a selectable gain path. Real attenuator selection and product limits require their own specified design.

observations.label: Receiver threshold gauge
observations.observed: Three printed marks accompany the gauge: sensitivity −14 dBm, maximum receive −1 dBm, and required reserve 2 dB. Receiver range includes both endpoints, while reserve is a separate requirement. A −13 dBm reading is above sensitivity but leaves only 1 dB reserve, so the declared exercise fails. No clue depends on the gauge’s colors.

observations.label: Wavelength-filter door
observations.observed: The door’s transparent leaves stand beside an ordinary walking entrance. They demonstrate a filter, not a lock requiring an ally or another media branch. Return to the gardens whenever you need to restore, inspect or change a candidate profile. A past preparation award does not establish the current connection’s condition.

observations.label: Link budget abacus
observations.observed: One row subtracts total loss from transmit power to give receive power in dBm. A second subtracts −14 dBm sensitivity from that receive level to give reserve in dB. These dimensions are different: −3 − 8 = −11, and −11 − (−14) = 3. Check the maximum independently. The later optional Prism Budget Bench is not required and awards no needed tool here.

observations.label: Power meter cradle
observations.observed: Place the ordinary inspection kit at the cradle and take a new reading for the selected path. Fresh means the same current configuration and attempt; after changing either, measure again. The notebook retains old results without silently refreshing them. A passing scoped optical budget supports this branch; it does not prove an end-to-end service.

observations.label: Module display case
observations.observed: Two complete route-kit trays sit beside a shell with the wrong physical profile. The Hermit Crab has labeled all three clearly: a convincing silhouette cannot replace a supported combination. Look at the cards, then use the compatibility chart and power ledger before validating either complete kit.

observations.label: SFP test cage
observations.observed: The cage accepts a familiar shell shape. Its host card is a separate document. “My house fitting through your door does not mean I can run your kitchen,” says the Hermit Crab. Read the selected module, medium, PHY, host and power requirements together.

observations.label: QSFP test cage
observations.observed: A many-laned diagram decorates the broad cage. The Chimera is proud of the diagram; it proves neither a particular supported rate nor a compatible host. The declared module and host profiles determine those facts.

observations.label: Delivered-power injector
observations.observed: The fictional label reads “30 W delivered to endpoints, after losses.” This is the comparison boundary for every demand card. The light indicates power; it does not announce a working data link or a successful application.

observations.label: Endpoint demand cards
observations.observed: The original three cards require 12 W, 11 W and 10 W. Total them before choosing a tray. Kit A uses the compatible 12 W and 11 W endpoints; kit B adds the supplied compatible 7 W endpoint. Both kits preserve their required route equipment; neither means discarding a mandatory tool to make the sum fit.

observations.label: Coaxial cross-section
observations.observed: The Badger taps the outer conductor with a pencil. “A cable has a history, and sometimes a very persuasive sales representative.” The cutaway illustrates a coaxial medium; its shape and history do not certify it for the route you are repairing.

observations.label: Telephone demarcation exhibit
observations.observed: A pair of wires disappears into an unplugged demonstration box. The Mole explains that an existing telephone medium has its own equipment context. Neither two wires nor a familiar plug establishes the required PHY, reach or host support for this repair.

observations.label: Equipment compatibility chart
observations.observed: Read each supplied row before testing the kit: form factor; PHY; medium; supported rate; host support; power method; each occupied port. A single failed row prevents readiness. The endpoint cards both negotiate: A advertises 1000/full and 100/full; B advertises 100/full and 10/half. Only 100/full appears in both.

observations.label: Power ledger
observations.observed: Keep the over-budget proposal visible while testing a replacement. Use the reusable inspection kit to capture the chosen kit’s current power and common-capability readings, check every compatibility row and occupied port, then submit that captured evidence. Compare 33 W before with 23 W or 30 W after. A label, button press or glowing lamp earns no equipment approval by itself.

observations.label: Loan counter
observations.observed: Borrow either complete kit and inspect it with the ordinary kit from your satchel. There is no fee or exhausted supply. You can return to the workshop, switch kits and test again. Help offers method, worked step and solution without a penalty. The Eel’s optional Energy Audit and the old maintenance record are separate errands.

observations.label: Master timing wheel
observations.observed: The wheel has all day. Its flags read “Pause whenever useful” and “There is no timing score.” Observe the sampling marks at your own pace; no rhythmic keypress opens the corridor.

observations.label: Untimed symbol loom
observations.observed: Start with the four supplied samples, inspect their mapping and enter the recovered bits. Step through each position or use the notebook and replay; both methods face the same checks. Choose the common mode and explain the physical role before submitting a captured current reading. The loom can show a sequence without claiming you decoded it.

observations.label: Four-level signal plinth
observations.observed: Read the complete teaching map: −3→00, −1→01, +1→10, +3→11. These are toy levels, not volts. Do not replace this map with a remembered real-PHY coding scheme.

observations.label: Common-capability console
observations.observed: Read both complete advertised lists. A: 1000/full, 100/full. B: 100/full, 10/half. Both negotiate. Choose their shared 100/full option, and keep unsupported options visibly unsupported. A matching color on the Chameleon is no substitute for this intersection.

observations.label: Infrared aperture
observations.observed: The Scorpion’s exhibit labels a physical signaling medium. It does not find an address, choose a route or log in to the distant beacon. Nothing essential is encoded only in a flash.

observations.label: Sampling gate
observations.observed: Four windows are labeled in order: position 0 shows −3; 1 shows +1; 2 shows +3; 3 shows −1. Inspect each window freely. Their order matters; how quickly you read them does not.

observations.label: Clock-recovery model
observations.observed: The Golem separates two placards: “when this receiver samples” and “what time it is.” This demonstration concerns physical sampling. It is neither a wall-clock synchronization service nor an address-discovery tool.

observations.label: Corridor toward the Backhoe Rift
observations.observed: The guard plate explains the preparation: prove one copper, fiber or radio route, check the equipment at the Shell Market and finish this calibration. Completing every branch is unnecessary. A gate opening is permission to investigate, not evidence that the damaged route or the Iron City’s services work. The workshop return is always available.

observations.label: Calibration dial
observations.observed: Inspect the labeled sample positions one at a time, or return to the notebook and replay the whole sequence. The dial is never timed. Your submitted answer still needs the current samples, supported common mode and physical-role explanation.

observations.label: Bit-pattern projector
observations.observed: One pane is reserved for your four-symbol decoding. A separate pane highlights NQ payload bytes inside a larger opaque upper-interface frame. The exercise answer and the NQ example are different; neither pane proves a login, route or full application service.
